questions.label: Meal timing
questions.claim: Skipping dinner resets your metabolism?
questions.prompt: What does the evidence say about skipping dinner as a metabolism reset?
options: It resets metabolism for good
It has not been shown to create a lasting reset
It always lowers energy use the next day
questions.explanation: Short studies show some changes in fuel use, not evidence of a lasting metabolic reset.
questions.caveat: These studies are short and do not establish what happens for every person over time.

sources.title: Impact of breakfast skipping compared with dinner skipping on regulation of energy balance and metabolic risk
sources.supports: A small randomized crossover study found no lower 24-hour energy expenditure from skipping dinner on the test day; it does not establish a lasting reset.

sources.title: Early Time-Restricted Feeding Reduces Appetite and Increases Fat Oxidation but Does Not Affect Energy Expenditure in Humans
sources.supports: A short feeding study found no significant change in 24-hour or resting energy expenditure, while some short-term fuel-use measures changed.

questions.label: Weight and willpower
questions.claim: Weight is mostly willpower?
questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects what can influence body weight?
options: Willpower is the only factor
Biology, habits, social conditions and surroundings can all play a part
One food explains everyone’s weight
questions.explanation: Body weight is not simply a matter of willpower. Biology, habits, social conditions and surroundings all play a part.
questions.caveat: No single factor explains everyone.

sources.title: WHO: Obesity and overweight
sources.supports: Describes obesity as shaped by interacting environmental, social, biological and behavioural determinants.

sources.title: NHLBI: Overweight and Obesity Causes and Risk Factors
sources.supports: Lists genetics, sleep, health conditions, behaviours and environmental factors among influences on weight.

questions.label: A short walk after a meal
questions.claim: A brief walk after a meal may reduce the blood-sugar rise for some people.
questions.prompt: What can a brief walk after a meal do for some people?
options: It may reduce the rise in blood sugar
It guarantees a normal reading
It replaces medical care
questions.explanation: A brief walk after a meal may reduce the blood-sugar rise for some people. Evidence for exactly ten minutes is limited.
questions.caveat: A small trial studied a glucose drink; a review found post-meal exercise may help, with limits in the evidence.

sources.title: Positive impact of a 10-min walk immediately after glucose intake on postprandial glucose levels
sources.supports: A small trial found lower glucose measures after a 10-minute walk following a glucose drink; the sample and setting limit generalization to meals.

sources.title: After Dinner Rest a While, After Supper Walk a Mile? A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis on the Acute Postprandial Glycemic Response to Exercise
sources.supports: A review of crossover trials found post-meal exercise reduced glucose excursions versus inactivity or pre-meal exercise, with limitations in the underlying evidence.

questions.label: Carbohydrates and blood sugar
questions.claim: Only sweets raise blood sugar?
questions.prompt: Which foods can raise blood sugar?
options: Only sweets
Sweets and starchy foods such as rice, roti and potatoes
Only fruit
questions.explanation: Sweets aren’t the only foods that can raise blood sugar. Rice, roti, potatoes and grains can too; there’s no need to avoid them all.
questions.caveat: Foods and individual responses differ.

sources.title: CDC: Carb Counting
sources.supports: Explains that both sugars and starches raise blood sugar and identifies grains and potatoes as starchy foods.

sources.title: American Diabetes Association: Understanding Carbs
sources.supports: Explains that carbohydrate foods break down into glucose and includes rice, whole-wheat bread and starchy vegetables.

questions.label: Before a diabetes diagnosis
questions.claim: Metabolic problems only affect people with diabetes?
questions.prompt: Can some metabolic risk factors be present before diabetes is diagnosed?
options: No, never
Yes, some can be present before diagnosis
Only after a person starts treatment
questions.explanation: Prediabetes and other cardiometabolic risk factors can be present before diabetes is diagnosed. This is not a diagnosis of anyone’s health.
questions.caveat: Only a qualified clinician can assess an individual.

sources.title: NIDDK: Insulin Resistance & Prediabetes
sources.supports: Defines prediabetes as glucose above normal but below the diabetes threshold and describes insulin resistance and associated conditions.

sources.title: ICMR-INDIAB-17: Metabolic non-communicable disease health report of India
sources.supports: Reports prediabetes as distinct from diabetes and separately measures cardiometabolic conditions including hypertension and dyslipidaemia in India.

questions.label: Sleep and appetite
questions.claim: Poor sleep can make you hungrier the next day.
questions.prompt: What might happen after a short night of sleep?
options: Some people may feel hungrier or eat more
Everyone loses their appetite
It always changes appetite hormones in the same way
questions.explanation: A short night may leave some people feeling hungrier or eating more the next day. Effects vary.
questions.caveat: Studies vary, and not everyone notices a change.

sources.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials of the Impact of Sleep Duration on Adiposity and Components of Energy Balance
sources.supports: Reports increased hunger and food intake in several sleep-restriction experiments while noting study variation and inconsistent appetite-hormone findings.

sources.title: A single night of moderate sleep restriction at-home increases hunger and food intake in overweight young adults
sources.supports: A small study observed greater hunger and food intake after one night of moderate sleep restriction; the sample and design limit generalization.

questions.label: Weight loss and muscle
questions.claim: Weight loss is only fat loss?
questions.prompt: Can weight loss include lean tissue as well as fat?
options: No, it is always only fat
Yes, it can include lean tissue
Only exercise causes any lean-tissue change
questions.explanation: Weight loss can reduce fat and lean tissue. Resistance exercise and enough protein may help preserve muscle, but results vary.
questions.caveat: Protein needs and suitable exercise vary by person.

sources.title: Preserving Healthy Muscle during Weight Loss
sources.supports: Reviews evidence that diet-induced weight loss can reduce muscle mass and that protein and physical activity, especially resistance exercise, may help preserve it.

sources.title: Effect of resistance exercise on body composition, muscle strength and cardiometabolic health during dietary weight loss
sources.supports: A systematic review and meta-analysis reports reductions in both fat and fat-free mass during dietary weight loss, with resistance exercise helping protect fat-free mass.

questions.label: Detox claims
questions.claim: A detox drink resets your metabolism?
questions.prompt: What has research shown about a special detox drink resetting metabolism?
options: It is proven to reset metabolism
No special drink has been shown to detoxify the body or reset metabolism
It works only when taken before breakfast
questions.explanation: No specific drink has been shown to reset metabolism or detoxify your body.
questions.caveat: Some cleanses may carry risks; this is general education.

sources.title: British Dietetic Association: Detox Diets
sources.supports: Explains that the body continually processes and removes waste and that no specific drink has been shown to provide a special detox effect.

sources.title: NCCIH: ‘Detoxes’ and ‘Cleanses’: What You Need To Know
sources.supports: Reports no compelling research that detox diets remove toxins and notes that some cleanses can carry risks.

questions.label: Whole fruit and juice
questions.claim: Fruit juice is the same as whole fruit?
questions.prompt: How is juice different from whole fruit?
options: Juice usually has less fibre and can be easier to drink in larger portions
Juice always contains more fibre
They are identical in every way
questions.explanation: Juice usually has less fibre and is easier to drink in larger portions. Whole fruit remains a healthy choice.
questions.caveat: Juice can affect blood sugar differently; foods and portions vary.

sources.title: WHO: Healthy diet
sources.supports: Recommends fruit as a carbohydrate source and notes that most fruit juices contain significant free sugars; it also emphasizes dietary fibre.

sources.title: NHS: 5 A Day: what counts?
sources.supports: Distinguishes whole-fruit portions from a capped 150 ml daily portion of juice or smoothies, noting that juice is easy to consume in excess.

questions.label: Fasting and health
questions.claim: Intermittent fasting is necessary for metabolic health?
questions.prompt: Is intermittent fasting required for metabolic health?
options: Yes, everyone needs it
No, it is one meal-timing approach, not a requirement
Yes, unless someone eats fruit
questions.explanation: Fasting is one way to time meals, not a requirement. Studies have not shown it superior to every other approach.
questions.caveat: Long-term evidence remains limited and responses differ.

sources.title: Is isocaloric intermittent fasting superior to calorie restriction? A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
sources.supports: A meta-analysis of 20 randomized trials concluded intermittent fasting may be an alternative to calorie restriction but was not superior overall; long-term evidence remains limited.

sources.title: Intermittent Fasting and Metabolic Health
sources.supports: Reviews possible benefits, comparable outcomes in some comparisons and heterogeneity in responses.

questions.label: Meal pairing and glucose response
questions.claim: Pairing carbohydrate foods with protein or fibre-rich foods can change how quickly glucose rises after a meal.
questions.prompt: With rice or roti, what can happen if the meal also includes dal, eggs or tofu, or fibre-rich vegetables?
options: The glucose rise may be slower or otherwise change
The glucose rise always becomes faster
The pairing never changes the glucose rise
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates raise glucose; protein- or fibre-containing foods can slow the rise. Pulse meals can also affect post-meal glucose (CDC; Hafiz et al.).
questions.caveat: The size and timing of any change vary with the foods, amounts, preparation and person; studies vary.

sources.title: Diabetes Meal Planning
sources.supports: The CDC says carbohydrate foods raise blood sugar and that eating them with protein-, fat- or fibre-containing foods slows how quickly it rises.

sources.title: Pulse consumption improves indices of glycemic control in adults with and without type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.supports: This review of randomized trials reports lower peak post-meal glucose after pulse intake, while noting inconsistent findings.

questions.label: Whole grains and refined grains
questions.claim: Many whole-grain foods provide more fibre than refined versions, and Indian guidance encourages including whole grains and millets in a varied diet.
questions.prompt: Which statement best matches general dietary guidance?
options: Many whole-grain foods provide more fibre than refined versions; Indian guidance encourages whole grains and millets
Refined grains generally provide more fibre; guidance encourages choosing refined grains
Whole- and refined-grain foods generally provide the same fibre
questions.explanation: Wholegrain choices such as brown rice and wholemeal bread are fibre sources; Indian guidance encourages whole grains and millets (NHS; ICMR-NIN).
questions.caveat: Fibre varies by grain, recipe and processing; this is a general pattern, not an individual glucose response.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians
sources.supports: ICMR-NIN recommends combining whole grains, cereals, pulses and millets, and preferring whole grains and millets to refined grains.

sources.title: Starchy foods and carbohydrates
sources.supports: The NHS says wholegrain varieties are good sources of fibre and that white bread has less fibre than wholegrain, wholemeal or brown bread.

questions.label: Ghee and saturated fat
questions.claim: Ghee is a source of saturated fat; WHO frames its guidance as a limit on saturated fat across the whole diet, not a ban on one food.
questions.prompt: Which statement best matches guidance on ghee and saturated fat?
options: Ghee contains saturated fat, and guidance considers saturated fat across the whole diet
Ghee has no saturated fat
WHO says everyone must avoid ghee completely
questions.explanation: Ghee is a source of saturated fat; WHO sets a limit for saturated fat across the diet, not a ban on ghee (WHO).
questions.caveat: Ghee content and portions vary. The WHO limit is diet-wide, not a ghee-specific serving target.

sources.title: WHO updates guidelines on fats and carbohydrates
sources.supports: WHO says saturated fat should provide no more than 10% of total energy for people aged 2 and older and identifies ghee among sources of saturated fat.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians
sources.supports: The ICMR-NIN guidelines identify ghee as a source of saturated fatty acids and advise limiting saturated-fat intake in adults.

questions.label: Cooking oils and energy density
questions.claim: Cooking oils are energy-dense, so guidance recommends using them in moderation—not avoiding all oils.
questions.prompt: Which statement best matches dietary guidance about cooking oils?
options: Use oils in moderation; unsaturated oils are generally preferred
Avoid every cooking oil because all oils are unhealthy
Use oils freely because plant oils provide little energy
questions.explanation: Oils are energy-dense, but fats are essential; guidance favors unsaturated oils and moderation rather than avoiding every oil (ICMR-NIN; WHO).
questions.caveat: Suitable amounts vary with energy needs, activity, life stage and the overall diet.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024
sources.supports: The ICMR-NIN guideline says visible cooking fats can be limited according to energy needs, while adequate good-quality fats are needed.

sources.title: Healthy diet
sources.supports: WHO says fat is essential, identifies unsaturated oils as preferable to saturated fats, and describes moderation as a core principle of healthy diets.

questions.label: Tea with meals and iron absorption
questions.claim: Tea consumed with a meal can reduce absorption of non-haem iron, especially iron from plant foods.
questions.prompt: What can happen when tea is consumed with a meal containing iron from plant foods?
options: It can reduce absorption of non-haem iron
It always increases non-haem iron absorption
It has no effect on absorption
questions.explanation: Tea with a rice meal reduced non-haem iron absorption in a study of young Indian women; effects can vary (ICMR-NIN; Thankachan et al.).
questions.caveat: The study measured short-term absorption from one meal in small groups; it does not predict long-term iron status for everyone.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024
sources.supports: ICMR-NIN guidance says tea can bind dietary iron and advises avoiding tea before, during or soon after meals.

sources.title: Iron absorption in young Indian women: the interaction of iron status with the influence of tea and ascorbic acid
sources.supports: In stable-isotope meal studies among young Indian women, black tea consumed with a rice meal decreased measured iron absorption.

questions.label: Plant protein variety
questions.claim: General guidance supports varied protein choices, including pulses and beans, soy foods, and dairy or eggs when included; no single food is mandatory.
questions.prompt: Which statement best matches general guidance on protein choices?
options: Vary protein foods: include pulses or beans and soy, with dairy or eggs if they fit your diet
Every vegetarian must eat eggs or dairy
One protein food is required for everyone
questions.explanation: Guidance names pulses, beans, soy, dairy and eggs among possible choices and encourages variety; no one food suits every diet (NHS; ICMR-NIN).
questions.caveat: Food needs vary with age, life stage and the overall diet; vegetarian diets need planning for nutrients beyond protein.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians: A Booklet
sources.supports: ICMR-NIN says vegetarians can meet protein needs with pulses, beans, peas and milk or curd, and recommends combining cereals with pulses.

sources.title: The vegetarian diet
sources.supports: NHS lists pulses, eggs, tofu and other meat alternatives as protein sources and recommends variety.

questions.label: Individual protein needs
questions.claim: One protein target does not fit everyone: needs can vary with age, health and life stage.
questions.prompt: Which statement is best?
options: Everyone needs the same protein amount
Protein needs can differ by age and health
Only activity level changes protein needs
questions.explanation: ICMR-NIN gives healthy adults a reference value and notes needs vary with age and physiological status.
questions.caveat: A population reference is not a personal target; illness, life stage and individual circumstances can change needs.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024
sources.supports: ICMR-NIN states protein needs vary with age, physiological status and stress, including infections, illness and physical stress.

sources.title: A Brief Note on Nutrient Requirements for Indians, the Recommended Dietary Allowances and Estimated Average Requirements (2020)
sources.supports: ICMR-NIN sets a reference for healthy Indian adults and lists differing recommendations for age groups, pregnancy and lactation.

questions.label: Strength exercise and muscle
questions.claim: Adult guidance recommends muscle-strengthening activity for major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week; resistance training can improve strength, but does not guarantee prevention of all muscle loss.
questions.prompt: Which statement best matches adult guidance and the evidence on strength?
options: Strengthen major muscle groups on 2 or more days; this can help strength but cannot promise to prevent all muscle loss
Strengthen major muscle groups once weekly; this is the adult guideline target
Strengthen every day; this guarantees muscle loss will not happen
questions.explanation: WHO recommends strengthening major muscle groups on 2 or more days weekly; resistance training can improve strength, but results vary (WHO).
questions.caveat: This is general adult guidance, not a guarantee; exercise suitability varies by person.

sources.title: Physical activity
sources.supports: WHO recommends adults do muscle-strengthening activities involving major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week.

sources.title: Resistance training prescription for muscle strength and hypertrophy in healthy adults: a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis
sources.supports: This review of trials in healthy adults found resistance-training prescriptions improved muscle strength compared with no exercise, with limitations in some comparisons.

questions.label: Breaking up sitting
questions.claim: For adults, replacing some sedentary time with physical activity—even light activity—is supported; no universal break schedule is established.
questions.prompt: What do guidelines support for adults who spend a lot of time sitting?
options: Replace some sitting with activity of any intensity, including light movement
Take a break every 30 minutes; that timing is proven for everyone
Replace sitting only with vigorous activity
questions.explanation: WHO recommends limiting sedentary time and replacing it with activity of any intensity, including light activity; it does not set a universal break schedule.
questions.caveat: Guidelines do not establish one break interval for everyone.

sources.title: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
sources.supports: WHO recommends that adults limit sedentary time and replace it with physical activity of any intensity, including light activity.

sources.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.supports: This guideline summary reports insufficient evidence to quantify a universal frequency or duration for sedentary breaks.

questions.label: Adult movement guidance
questions.claim: WHO recommends adults do 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week and muscle-strengthening activity on 2 or more days each week.
questions.prompt: Which weekly activity target matches WHO guidance for adults?
options: 150–300 minutes moderate aerobic activity, plus strength work on 2 or more days
75 minutes moderate aerobic activity, plus strength work once a week
300 minutes moderate aerobic activity every day, with no strength work
questions.explanation: WHO recommends 150–300 moderate minutes weekly plus strength work on 2+ days; this is guidance, not a guarantee of an outcome.
questions.caveat: Benefits vary; meeting a target does not guarantee a specific metabolic or health outcome.

sources.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour: Recommendations
sources.supports: The adult recommendation specifies 150–300 weekly minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity and strengthening involving all major muscle groups on 2 or more days weekly.

sources.title: Physical activity
sources.supports: WHO's official guidance page describes weekly moderate activity and strengthening on 2 or more days.

questions.label: South Asian risk patterns
questions.claim: South Asian populations can have increased cardiometabolic risk at lower BMI than standard cutoffs suggest, but BMI alone does not determine an individual’s health.
questions.prompt: Which statement is best supported?
options: South Asian groups may have higher risk at lower BMI on average, but BMI alone cannot determine an individual’s health
A standard-range BMI rules out higher risk for South Asians
Every South Asian person has the same risk at one fixed BMI
questions.explanation: South Asian groups can face higher diabetes and heart-disease risk at lower BMI on average; BMI alone is not a personal diagnosis.
questions.caveat: These are population patterns, not a prediction for every person; risk varies and evidence does not support one universal cutoff.

sources.title: South Asian American Perspectives on Overweight, Obesity, and the Relationship Between Weight and Health
sources.supports: This CDC-published article reports that South Asian adults can develop type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease at lower BMI than some other groups.

sources.title: Obesity and Cardiovascular Risk among South Asian Americans
sources.supports: This review says South Asian cardiovascular and metabolic risks can be increased at BMI levels considered normal, while noting limitations in defining cutoffs.

questions.label: Waist and risk
questions.claim: A larger waist can be associated with higher cardiometabolic risk, but waist size alone does not determine an individual’s health.
questions.prompt: What can waist size tell us about cardiometabolic risk?
options: It tells someone's risk exactly on its own
It can be one clue linked with higher risk, but it is not a diagnosis
It has no link with cardiometabolic risk
questions.explanation: Waist circumference can signal higher risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes, but it cannot diagnose a person by itself.
questions.caveat: Risk patterns vary; waist is one marker, not a complete health assessment.

sources.title: Aim for a Healthy Weight — National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute
sources.supports: The NHLBI says fat carried around the waist is linked with higher risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.

sources.title: Waist circumference and cardiometabolic risk: a consensus statement from Shaping America’s Health
sources.supports: This consensus statement reports that waist circumference relates to diabetes and coronary heart disease risk, while noting uncertainty about added predictive value.

questions.label: Adult sleep duration
questions.claim: For adults aged 18–60, consensus guidance recommends 7 or more hours of sleep regularly to support health, while individual sleep needs can vary.
questions.prompt: For adults aged 18–60, which statement best matches sleep guidance?
options: Regularly aim for 7 or more hours; individual needs can vary
Regularly aim for fewer than 6 hours; needs are the same
Regularly aim for exactly 9 hours; needs do not vary
questions.explanation: AASM/SRS recommend 7 or more hours regularly for adults aged 18–60 to promote health, while noting sleep needs vary.
questions.caveat: This is general guidance, not an exact target or guarantee for each person.

sources.title: About Sleep
sources.supports: Lists 7 or more hours daily for adults aged 18–60 and says enough sleep supports health.

sources.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society
sources.supports: Recommends adults aged 18–60 sleep 7 or more hours regularly to promote health and notes individual variability in sleep need.

questions.label: Sleep and general health
questions.claim: Enough, good-quality sleep on a regular schedule supports general health.
questions.prompt: Which statement is best supported by health guidance?
options: Enough, good-quality sleep on a regular schedule supports general health
Sleep matters only when someone wants to lose weight
A single short night always causes lasting health problems
questions.explanation: Sleep is important for health and well-being; enough sleep, quality and a steady schedule are all parts of healthy sleep (CDC; NIH).
questions.caveat: Sleep needs vary. Guidance does not treat sleep as a weight-loss treatment or guarantee.

sources.title: About Sleep
sources.supports: CDC says good sleep is essential for health and emotional well-being, and recommends a regular bedtime and wake time.

sources.title: Good Sleep for Good Health
sources.supports: NIH describes sleep as important for good health and identifies sleep amount, quality and a consistent schedule as parts of healthy sleep.

questions.label: Added sugars and drinks
questions.claim: Indian NIN guidance says to avoid foods and drinks with added sugars; WHO identifies free sugars as a key risk factor for tooth decay.
questions.prompt: Which statement best matches Indian and WHO guidance?
options: Avoid foods and drinks with added sugars; free sugars are a tooth-decay risk factor
Sweetened drinks are recommended as a regular source of free sugars
Only sugar added at home counts as free sugar
questions.explanation: India’s NIN advises avoiding foods and drinks with added sugars; WHO identifies free sugars as a tooth-decay risk (ICMR-NIN; WHO).
questions.caveat: This is general guidance, not a personal restriction or an individual health assessment.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024
sources.supports: The Indian NIN guideline advises avoiding foods and beverages with added sugars.

sources.title: Sugars and dental caries
sources.supports: WHO identifies free sugars in foods and beverages as a major tooth-decay risk factor.

questions.label: Dietary fibre sources
questions.claim: Vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains are commonly named sources of dietary fibre.
questions.prompt: Which group includes common sources of dietary fibre?
options: Vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains
Milk, eggs, fish and meat
Oils, butter, sugar and sweet drinks
questions.explanation: Official guidance names vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains among fibre-containing foods; amounts vary across foods (ICMR-NIN; WHO).
questions.caveat: This identifies sources, not a personal intake target; recommendations vary by age and guidance.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians
sources.supports: The ICMR-NIN guideline describes fibre in vegetables, fruits, whole grains and pulses.

sources.title: Healthy diet
sources.supports: WHO identifies whole grains, vegetables, fruit and pulses as carbohydrate sources and mentions naturally occurring fibre.

questions.label: More than one number
questions.claim: A scale number alone does not give a full picture of metabolic health.
questions.prompt: Which statement best matches health guidance?
options: One scale number gives the full picture
A fuller picture uses several measures, such as waist, blood pressure and blood tests
How someone feels is the only measure
questions.explanation: Guidance considers several measures, including waist, blood pressure and blood tests; BMI is a screening measure, not the whole picture (NHS; CDC).
questions.caveat: This is general education, not an assessment. Guidance does not mean everyone needs every test.

sources.title: Metabolic syndrome — NHS
sources.supports: The NHS describes metabolic syndrome as a group of health problems and lists checks including BMI, waist, blood pressure, blood glucose and blood fats.

sources.title: About Body Mass Index (BMI) — CDC
sources.supports: The CDC says BMI is a screening measure and should be considered with other factors, including blood pressure, cholesterol, glucose and medical history.

questions.label: Weight maintenance and support
questions.claim: Maintaining weight loss can be challenging; ongoing habits and support may help, but regain is not inevitable.
questions.prompt: After losing weight, which statement is best supported?
options: Keeping it off can be challenging; habits and support may help, and experiences differ
Everyone regains weight, whatever support they have
Once weight is lost, it stays off without ongoing habits
questions.explanation: Maintaining weight can be challenging; habits and support may help, but outcomes differ and regain is not certain (CDC; BMJ).
questions.caveat: Evidence is limited beyond two years and much of the research is from the US and Scandinavia.

sources.title: Tips for Keeping Weight Off
sources.supports: CDC says maintaining habits after weight loss can be challenging and describes ongoing eating patterns, activity, monitoring and support among people who maintain weight loss.

sources.title: Long term maintenance of weight loss with non-surgical interventions in obese adults: systematic review and meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials
sources.supports: This review found comprehensive behavioural interventions moderately slowed regain through up to 24 months, with limited evidence beyond that period.

questions.label: Safety and shared decisions
questions.claim: A health decision can consider evidence and the person’s individual needs, values and preferences.
questions.prompt: When asking whether a health approach is safe and right for you, what is most useful?
options: Discuss the evidence, possible benefits and harms, and your situation with a qualified clinician
Use the same answer for everyone
Decide from one online quiz
questions.explanation: NICE describes shared decisions as weighing evidence with a person’s needs, preferences and values, including discussion of risks and benefits.
questions.caveat: This game cannot assess personal safety or replace a conversation with a clinician.

sources.title: Shared decision making — NICE guideline NG197
sources.supports: NICE recommends healthcare professionals and people using services work together on treatment and care decisions, including communicating risks and benefits.

sources.title: About shared decision making — NICE
sources.supports: NICE says treatment choices should be based on evidence and the person’s individual preferences, beliefs and values.

questions.label: Safety beyond diabetes
questions.claim: Not having diabetes does not establish that a health approach is safe for you.
questions.prompt: Does not having diabetes by itself tell you whether a health approach is safe for you?
options: Yes; diabetes is the only factor that matters
No; safety depends on your situation, and some risks can exist before diagnosis
Yes; a quiz can confirm it
questions.explanation: Safety depends on your health context; some metabolic risks can exist before diabetes is diagnosed. A quiz cannot assess personal safety.
questions.caveat: This is general education, not an eligibility test or diagnosis.

sources.title: Shared decision making — NICE guideline NG197
sources.supports: NICE recommends discussing treatment and care options in light of individual needs and circumstances.

sources.title: NIDDK: Insulin Resistance & Prediabetes
sources.supports: Prediabetes is a glucose risk state distinct from a diabetes diagnosis; this does not determine anyone’s individual health.

questions.label: No one-size-fits-all safety answer
questions.claim: A quiz cannot establish that a health approach is safe for every person.
questions.prompt: Can one quiz tell you whether a health approach is safe for everyone?
options: Yes, the same answer fits every person
No; discuss options and your circumstances with a clinician
Yes, if the quiz gives a high score
questions.explanation: NICE recommends shared decisions that consider evidence alongside the individual’s needs and preferences; a quiz cannot assess those for you.
questions.caveat: This is a boundary of the game, not a judgment about any particular treatment.

sources.title: Shared decision making — NICE guideline NG197
sources.supports: NICE says decisions about treatment and care should be made together in light of individual needs and circumstances.

sources.title: About shared decision making — NICE
sources.supports: NICE says treatment choices should account for personal preferences and involve discussing risks, benefits and possible outcomes.

questions.label: Before a diabetes diagnosis
questions.claim: Some glucose and cardiometabolic risk factors can exist before a person is diagnosed with diabetes.
questions.prompt: Can a person have a glucose risk state before a diabetes diagnosis?
options: Yes; prediabetes is distinct from diabetes
No; there is no state before diabetes
Only after someone starts treatment
questions.explanation: NIDDK describes prediabetes as glucose above normal but below the diabetes threshold; it is not itself a diabetes diagnosis.
questions.caveat: Only a qualified clinician can interpret an individual’s tests and health history.

sources.title: NIDDK: Insulin Resistance & Prediabetes
sources.supports: Defines prediabetes as glucose above normal but below the diabetes threshold and describes it as distinct from diabetes.

sources.title: ICMR-INDIAB-17: Metabolic non-communicable disease health report of India
sources.supports: Reports prediabetes separately from diabetes and measures other cardiometabolic conditions in India.

questions.label: Weight returning is not inevitable
questions.claim: Weight regain can happen, but it is not inevitable and is not a personal failure.
questions.prompt: Does everyone regain weight after losing it?
options: Yes, it always happens
No; maintenance can be challenging, but experiences differ
No; weight never returns once lost
questions.explanation: Maintaining weight can be difficult for some, but outcomes differ; ongoing habits and support may help (CDC; BMJ).
questions.caveat: No approach guarantees a particular long-term result.

sources.title: Tips for Keeping Weight Off
sources.supports: CDC says maintenance is challenging but describes people who maintain weight loss with continued habits and support.

sources.title: Long term maintenance of weight loss with non-surgical interventions in obese adults: systematic review and meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials
sources.supports: The review found that comprehensive behavioral support can slow regain in trials through up to 24 months, with uncertainty beyond that.

questions.label: Starches count too
questions.claim: Starchy foods such as rice, roti and potatoes can raise blood sugar too.
questions.prompt: Which kinds of foods can raise blood sugar?
options: Only sweet foods
Sugars and starches, including rice, roti and potatoes
Only foods that taste sweet
questions.explanation: Both sugars and starches can raise blood sugar; rice, grains and potatoes are examples of starchy foods (CDC; ADA).
questions.caveat: This is not a reason to avoid all carbohydrate foods; foods and individual responses differ.

sources.title: CDC: Carb Counting
sources.supports: Explains that both sugars and starches raise blood sugar and identifies grains and potatoes as starchy foods.

sources.title: American Diabetes Association: Understanding Carbs
sources.supports: Explains that carbohydrate foods break down into glucose and includes rice and starchy vegetables.
